Fixed in commit 13 (`c8a83922`), recorded as BLG-280.

A dial address is now exactly three parts and nothing else: a host (`ip4` or `ip6` that is not unspecified, multicast or broadcast, or `dns`/`dns4`/`dns6`), a TCP port from 1024 up, and `/p2p/<id>`, where the id must be the one derived from the validator key that announces it. Nested addresses, a second host, a low port and a foreign peer id are refused in `check_tx`, so they never reach a block. Invite peers follow the same rule.

What stays, on purpose: private and loopback hosts are still accepted, because a Garden is meant to run on one local network and the acceptance scenario runs on `127.0.0.1`. What a member can still cause is one TCP connection to a port >= 1024 that it names, carrying the multistream header and closed when the Noise identity does not match; redials back off (BLG-277).

### ~~Garden block timestamp has no upper bound, so one leading validator can halt the chain permanently~~

**Resolved** — no longer flagged as of `7f0fd29`.

Fixed in commit 19 (`7f0fd295`), recorded as BLG-291. Two checks.

1. In the state machine (`verify_block`, `build_header`): one block moves the chain clock forward by at most `MAX_BLOCK_TIMESTAMP_STEP_MS`. A header at `u64::MAX` is refused, and no single block can use up the range.
2. At the vote (`consider`): no validator signs a block dated more than `MAX_TIMESTAMP_AHEAD_MS` (two minutes) ahead of its own clock. The host signs every block, so one leader cannot move the chain to a time nobody has reached.

The step is one year and not the suggested 60 seconds, on purpose. A Garden writes a block only when there is something to write, and it can stand frozen for days. With a 60 second step the first block after an idle hour would be dated 59 minutes in the past, the chain clock would never catch up, and every time the feed shows would be wrong. The step keeps the range from being used up; the comparison with a clock at the vote keeps the timestamp true.

Red first: `garden_block_timestamp_cannot_use_up_the_clock`, `garden_validator_does_not_sign_a_block_dated_ahead_of_its_clock`.

### ~~Garden publication share is charged with the sender-asserted `Publish.size`, so one validator can pin ~256 GiB on every peer's disk~~

**Resolved** — no longer flagged as of `a3c1b7f`.

Fixed in commit 19 (`7f0fd295`), recorded as BLG-292. The layer that was missing is there now: a node keeps bytes for a publication only when they have the size the publication declares.

- Deposited bytes (`PutObject`) leave the evictable queue only when a finalized publication accounts for their size. Bytes of another size stay a deposit under the quota of the peer that deposited them (8 objects for one peer, 64 in all), and its next deposits push them out.
- Bytes a holder fetches are kept only when a publication declares their size. Otherwise they are dropped, the measured size is noted, and the object is not asked for again until a publication accounts for it. So a false size cannot be turned into repeated 4 MiB downloads either.
- Resolving such content answers "this content does not have the size its publication declares".

The bytes a validator leaves pinned on a peer are now at most the bytes it was charged for, so the share is a ceiling on bytes again.

**On commit 17.** Commit 17 on this branch took the suggested change and charged `max_object_bytes` for every publication. Commit 19 puts the charge back to the declared size, for one reason: at the default limits (share 256 MiB, object 4 MiB) the whole-object charge leaves a validator 64 publications for the life of a Garden, short messages included. A room where each person can say 64 things is not what the share is for. With the declaration checked by every node that would store the bytes, the whole-object charge bounds nothing that is not bounded already. `garden_small_publications_are_charged_by_their_size_not_as_whole_objects` holds this: it publishes one message more than `share / max_object_bytes`.

Red first: `garden_publication_that_understates_its_size_does_not_keep_its_bytes` (deposit path red on the previous head; fetch path red with the check switched off).

Answered in commit 19 (`7f0fd295`), recorded as BLG-290. The finding is right about the mechanism. The damage it leads to is closed; the suggested bound is not taken, and this is why.

**What the mechanism could do, measured.** Every block needs the host's signature, and since BLG-285 the host, like every validator, does not sign a report on a validator it still hears. So a leader that is not the host cannot release anybody the host hears. What remains is the host itself: when it leads, a block that reports everybody else needs its one signature. With that block and one more (its own `Leave`, which retired the Garden because no validator was Active any more) the host made every other node wipe its content and stop, while those nodes were still there. That is reproduced by `garden_end_does_not_wipe_a_validator_that_never_left` (red on the previous head: `Err("garden node has stopped")`) and it is closed: a node the chain holds as Suspended never signed a departure, so the end of the Garden no longer stops it or clears its disk. It keeps what it holds, readable, until its own `leave`.

**Why not `electorate * 3 > active * 2`.** Section 3 of the Garden directive has three rules that this bound breaks: "the Garden chain runs as long as the host is connected" (3.2), "when a validator other than the host leaves abruptly the chain does not stop" (3.4, V-1), "everyone leaves and returns whenever they want" (3.8).
- With 2 or 3 active validators the bound refuses every report (`1*3 <= 2*2`, `2*3 <= 3*2`), while `quorum(2) == 2` and `quorum(3) == 3`. One phone going dark halts a Garden of two or three for good, with the host connected.
- With 4, two validators gone at once leave two present and `quorum(3) == 3`: halted, host connected. In general any third of the validators ends the Garden for the rest by going silent, and nobody new gets in, because a `Join` needs a block.
- During a freeze nothing can be written, so validators that leave then leave no record. The host has to be able to return to whoever is still there: `garden_host_returns_after_validators_left_the_frozen_garden`, written for an earlier finding on this PR.

Absence cannot be proven to a state machine. The evidence is a signature that is not there, and whoever builds the block decides which signatures are in it. So a rule that lets the chain go on without the silent ones also lets the block builder call a present validator silent, and a rule that prevents the second stops the first. The directive says which side to take: the host is the one validator the chain depends on.

**What the host can and cannot do now.** It can stop counting a validator. That is no more than it can do by withholding its signature from every block that carries that validator's transactions, or by leaving. The report is a transaction signed by the leader, in a block signed by the host, on the chain for every participant to read (`bud_gardenTrace`). The released validator keeps its content, re-enters with its own `Resume` (its node sends it by itself), and is never made to delete anything. Nothing can be done in its name: every other transaction kind is signed by its sender.

Rule 3.3 says the host has no other authority. This is the one place where 3.2 and 3.3 pull apart, and it is reported to the owner as such. If the owner prefers the bound and accepts the halts, it is one check in `execute`.

Fixed in commit 19 (`7f0fd295`), recorded as BLG-293, with the suggested bound and one more check.

- `verify_votes` refuses a commit that carries more votes than its electorate has validators, before the first signature is checked.
- A second vote of the same validator is refused before it is verified, so a list of the right length cannot be padded with repeats either.

So one commit costs at most one signature check per validator of the Garden. Red first on the previous head: `garden_commit_takes_one_vote_from_each_validator` (the padded list and the repeated voter were both accepted; the last case shows the count is taken before any signature).

### 🔵 Garden member chooses the TCP endpoint every other validator dials, before its peer id is checked

**Severity:** LOW · Deep review

**TL;DR:** `dial_known` dials any shape-valid address a member wrote into `Join`/`Resume`, so one member can make every other member's node open outbound connections to any host and port it names, not the one it answers at.

**Impact:** A member holding the invite can aim every other member's node at any internal host:port (private range, loopback, link-local, or a `/dns` name the victim resolves), so co-members' machines issue TCP connections and multistream/Noise bytes into networks the attacker cannot reach itself.

**Root cause:**
- The trust boundary is drawn at address shape instead of at endpoint: an announced address is only checked to be one host, a TCP port from 1024 up and the announcer's own peer id, and nothing establishes that the address reaches the announcer before other nodes dial it.
- `dial_known` takes the host and port from the ledger record the validator itself wrote and hands them to the swarm with `DialOpts::unknown_peer_id()`, so the TCP connection is established and the Noise exchange starts before the id in the address is ever compared.
- The same unverified address is exported in the invite line and in invite peers, so a node that just joined dials a member-chosen endpoint before it knows anything about the Garden.

<details><summary>Prompt to fix with AI</summary>

`````markdown
This is a security vulnerability found during a code review.

Vulnerability: Garden member chooses the TCP endpoint every other validator dials, before its peer id is checked
Severity: LOW
CWE: CWE-918

**TL;DR:** `dial_known` dials any shape-valid address a member wrote into `Join`/`Resume`, so one member can make every other member's node open outbound connections to any host and port it names, not the one it answers at.

**Impact:** A member holding the invite can aim every other member's node at any internal host:port (private range, loopback, link-local, or a `/dns` name the victim resolves), so co-members' machines issue TCP connections and multistream/Noise bytes into networks the attacker cannot reach itself.

**Root cause:**
`````

Answered in commit 20 (`bf9d7982`), recorded as BLG-299. This one needed a product decision, and the owner made it: a Garden has two admission modes, chosen by the host at creation and fixed in the genesis.

- `direct`: anyone who holds the link or QR is seated at once. The invite is a bearer credential here, and that is the definition of the mode, so what you describe stays possible in it: the holder of the link is a member and can bring more keys. The host that does not want this picks the other mode.
- `host_approval`: a `Join` with a valid invite only records a request. The key is `Waiting`: no seat, no vote, no share, no leadership, not in the electorate, cannot publish, and no node dials it. The host answers with a new transaction, `Admit { target, accept }`. Only the host can send it, only while the Garden runs. Accept seats the key; reject removes the record and leaves the nonce, so the old signed request cannot be replayed by anyone.

In `host_approval` a node also serves content bytes only to seated keys. The waiting list is bounded by `max_validators` and takes no seat.

Surface: `bud_gardenCreate` takes `"admission"`, `bud_gardenAdmit [key, accept]` is on the operator listener only, and status shows `admission`, `waiting_for_host` and `me.turned_away`.

- A waiting or rejected invite holder still follows blocks (that is how it learns the answer), so block metadata is visible to it. Content bytes are not. Recorded as BLG-307.
- An invite holder can fill the waiting list with generated keys. That slows admission, it gives no seat and no vote. Recorded as BLG-308.

### 🟡 Garden: 16 half-open TCP sockets exhaust the pre-handshake connection budget and shut the node's invite path

**Severity:** MEDIUM · Deep review

**TL;DR:** `start_with` in `src/garden/net.rs` caps pending inbound upgrades at 16 and puts no deadline on the connection setup, so 16 TCP peers that send no Noise bytes make the node refuse every further inbound connection, invited joins included.

**Impact:** Anyone with a route to a Garden node's listen port — LAN peer, port scanner, or an existing member — holds those 16 slots with idle sockets, and the node then accepts no new connection: invited validators cannot reach the host to join, and members cannot dial a node whose link dropped.

**Root cause:**
- ["The door is bounded only by counting pending libp2p upgrades: `libp2p::connection_limits` takes a slot when the TCP socket is accepted, before one byte of the multistream/Noise handshake, and gives it back only when that setup finishes or fails.", "Nothing bounds how long the setup may take — `with_tcp` builds the transport with no `TransportTimeout`, and `with_idle_connection_timeout` only covers connections that already finished the upgrade.", "Garden's own stranger logic is blind to these sockets: `drop_strangers` and `MAX_UNADMITTED` run on `NetEvent::Connected`, which is emitted from `ConnectionEstablished`, and `Swarm::close_connection` refuses a connection that is still pending."]

```suggestion

            let transport = tcp::tokio::Transport::new(tcp::Config::default())
                .upgrade(libp2p::core::upgrade::Version::V1Lazy)
                .authenticate(noise::Config::new(key).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?)
                .multiplex(yamux::Config::default())
                .boxed();
            Ok::<_, Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>>(
                libp2p::core::transport::timeout::TransportTimeout::with_ingoing_timeout(
                    transport,
                    Duration::from_secs(10),
                ),
            )
        })
        .map_err(|e| format!("garden transport cannot start: {e}"))?
```
